scenes.title: Correlated Subqueries
scenes.narration: A correlated subquery is an inner query that depends on a column from the outer query, so it must be evaluated once for every outer row.

scenes.title: What makes a subquery correlated
bullets: The inner query references a column from the outer query.
It cannot run on its own because it needs the outer row's value.
It is re-evaluated for each row the outer query processes.
scenes.narration: The defining trait is that the inner query mentions a column belonging to the outer query. This means the subquery cannot be run in isolation, since it needs a value from the current outer row. As a result the database re-executes the subquery for every single row the outer query examines.

scenes.title: Row by row evaluation
steps: Outer query picks the next row
Its column value is passed into the inner query
Inner query runs using that value
Outer row is kept or discarded based on the result
scenes.narration: For each row the outer query considers, its column value is handed to the inner subquery. The subquery runs using that value and produces a result. The outer row is then kept or discarded, and the whole cycle repeats for the next row.

scenes.title: Earning more than the department average
scenes.code:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(s.salary)
    FROM employees s
    WHERE s.dept_id = e.dept_id
);
scenes.narration: Notice that the inner query references e.dept_id, which belongs to the outer employees table aliased as e. For each outer employee, the subquery computes the average salary of only that employee's own department. The outer query keeps the employee if their salary beats that department specific average, so the benchmark changes from row to row.

scenes.title: Departments that have at least one employee
scenes.code:
SELECT d.dept_id, d.dept_name
FROM departments d
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM employees e
    WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id
);
scenes.narration: Correlated subqueries pair naturally with EXISTS, which returns true as soon as the inner query finds a single matching row. Here, for each department the subquery checks whether any employee shares that department id. EXISTS stops at the first match, which makes it efficient for existence checks compared with counting rows.

scenes.title: EXISTS versus NOT EXISTS

left.title: EXISTS
points: True when the inner query returns any row
Short circuits at the first match

right.title: NOT EXISTS
points: True when the inner query returns no rows
Finds empty departments with no employees
Useful for anti joins and missing data

scenes.narration: EXISTS succeeds the moment the correlated subquery finds a matching row, which is why it works well for confirming that related data is present. NOT EXISTS flips the logic and succeeds only when no matching rows are found, making it ideal for spotting orphaned or missing records. Both benefit from short circuiting rather than scanning the entire related set.

scenes.text: Because the inner query runs once per outer row, correlated subqueries can be costly on large tables. Ensure the correlated column is indexed, and consider a JOIN when the optimizer cannot rewrite it.
scenes.narration: Since the subquery is re-evaluated for every outer row, it can become expensive as tables grow. Index the correlated column, and if performance suffers consider rewriting the query as a join.
